_meta.title: Naming-System Starter Packs
_meta.purpose: Ready-to-use data for the naming engine. Two independent pack types: phonetic element packs (sound-building blocks, grouped by phonaesthetic mood) and semantic concept packs (meaning slots, additive by theme).

how_they_fit.phonetic_element_packs: Feed Step 3 (generation architecture) and the phonaesthetics dial. Each pack supplies start / middle / end elements for one mood. A seeded language samples a SUBSET of a pack (especially a tight subset of endings) for per-culture cohesion.
how_they_fit.semantic_concept_packs: Feed Step 4 (word roots). 'core' is the universal set every culture draws on. Thematic packs are ADDITIVE on top of core, never replacements. A culture may stack several (e.g. core + warrior + seafaring). Each concept is minted into a form using the CULTURE'S OWN phonology at seed time, so the same concept sounds different in every language.

_meta.joinery_rules: start and middle elements end in a vowel OR a sonorant (l, r, n); middle and end elements begin with a consonant. Every seam therefore closes vowel-or-sonorant onto a consonant onset, which never produces a vowel pile-up and never welds an unpronounceable cluster: a sonorant coda leads cleanly into any onset (Gorn-drak, Kar-tha). Cluster-INITIAL middles and ends (gda, kta, dko) are legal because the seam splits them across the syllable boundary (Ka+gda = Kag-da). Start elements get no such rescue — nothing precedes them — so their onsets must be legal English onsets or carry a named waiver (see readability_note). The 'grand' and 'exotic' moods keep their open vowels and diphthongs immediately after the onset consonant, so character is preserved without breaking the rule.
_meta.readability_note: Two separate constraints, not one: the 26-LETTER constraint governs letters (no gratuitous apostrophes, no accents, no x-for-z), while the CLUSTER rules govern sounds (legal onsets, seam joinery). All elements pass both, verified by pack_validator.py as a build step — packs must be re-validated whenever edited. Start-vowel policy: A/E/I open freely; O needs a following consonant (a single one is fine — Oliver, Omar, Oona — but O+vowel fails); U needs a following cluster (Ulric); initial Y and triple-vowel openings fail. NAMED WAIVERS — deliberate mood-edge onsets kept intentionally: ts- (familiar via tsar/tsunami, exotic) and vr- (marginal via vroom, harsh). Anything not waived must be a legal English onset; zg- marks where the line is. Elements that coincide with real given names (Ava, Mae, Kai) are acceptable because elements are not names — the collision gate runs on assembled output. Genre-established borrowings (grim, dun, bra as onset) are likewise waived.
_meta.weighting_note: Selection frequency is by list multiplicity. Base packs therefore ship DUPLICATE-FREE, so that duplication remains the reserved, unambiguous weighting signal: to make a mood or theme dominate a culture, duplicate its entries rather than adding code. Applying a thematic pack also raises the frequency of its concepts in generated names, not just their availability.

revision.summary: All five phonetic packs run through the Step 6 gates (pack_validator.py); 14 failures corrected, joinery rule extended to sonorant finals, waiver mechanism made explicit. Assembly smoke-test additionally caught Oba+mor = "Obamor" (assembled-name collision), corrected to Orda — evidence that the collision gate must run on assembled output, not elements. Second validation pass added a final-coda gate (J1: -aw/-ew/-ow only) after -raew escaped the first pass.

rescued_by_rule_refinement.note: These violated the original vowel-final joinery rule but are phonologically sound; the amended sonorant-final rule (l/r/n) legalises them rather than deleting good data.

harsh.description: Hard and forceful. Stops (k, g, t, d, p, b), consonant clusters, closed syllables.
harsh.why: Stops halt the airflow abruptly, so names feel clipped and aggressive.

soft.description: Smooth and flowing. Liquids (l, r), nasals (m, n), open vowels, open syllables.
soft.why: Air keeps moving through these sounds, so names feel unbroken and gentle.

bright.description: Sharp and keen. Front vowels (i, e) and sibilants (s, sh).
bright.why: Front vowels and hissing sounds read as small, quick and bright (the 'kiki' end of sound-symbolism).

grand.description: Weighty and old. Open back vowels (a, o) and longer forms.
grand.why: Big open vowels and length feel slow and heavy, so names feel ancient and large.

exotic.description: Foreign but readable. Diphthongs (ae, oi, eu) and combinations uncommon in English.
exotic.why: Sounds English rarely uses read as foreign, while staying pronounceable enough for the reader.

core.description: The universal set every culture draws on: auspicious traits, kinship, and common descriptive elements. 70 concepts; stacking one or two thematic packs brings a culture to the ~100-root figure the research recommends. Always active.

warrior.description: For martial cultures. War, weapons, courage, and conquest. Additive on top of core.

seafaring.description: For maritime and coastal cultures. Sea, tide, weather, and voyage. Additive on top of core.

mountain.description: For highland, delving, and mountain-fastness cultures. Additive on top of core.

forest.description: For woodland, wild, and sylvan cultures. Additive on top of core.

arcane.description: For magical, scholarly, and mystic cultures. Additive on top of core.

desert.description: For desert, nomad, and sun-scoured cultures. Additive on top of core.

mercantile.description: For trading, guild, and urban cultures. Additive on top of core.

priestly.description: For religious, temple, and devotional cultures. Additive on top of core.

agrarian.description: For farming, pastoral, and hearth-bound cultures. Additive on top of core.
